reading.title: The Lighthouse Cat
reading.text:
Nobody knew where the cat had come from. One stormy evening, she simply appeared on the steps of the old lighthouse, soaked and shivering, and stared up at Mr Pereira as if she had been expecting him.
Mr Pereira had kept the lighthouse for thirty years, and he did not like surprises. Still, he could not leave her outside. He wrapped her in a towel and gave her a saucer of warm milk. “Just for tonight,” he muttered.
But the cat stayed. Each night she climbed the hundred and twelve steps beside him and sat by the great lamp, watching the dark sea. Mr Pereira began to talk to her about the ships and the weather. He named her Beacon.
One foggy night, Beacon would not settle. She paced and yowled at the window until Mr Pereira looked out. Far below, a small fishing boat was drifting towards the rocks. He sounded the foghorn just in time, and the boat turned away.
After that, Mr Pereira never said “just for tonight” again.

reading.title: Mangrove Forests
reading.text:
Along the coast of the United Arab Emirates grow strange-looking forests: mangroves. Mangrove trees can live in salty water that would kill most other plants. Their tangled roots stick up out of the mud like hundreds of pencils. These roots help the trees to breathe when the tide comes in and covers the mud.
Mangroves are important for many reasons. Their roots make a safe nursery for young fish and crabs, which hide from bigger animals among the roots below the water. Birds such as herons and flamingos visit to feed. The trees also protect the coast. When storms bring strong waves, the thick roots slow the water down and stop the land from being washed away.
Today, people are planting new mangroves to help these forests grow. Visitors can paddle through them in kayaks, as long as they are careful not to disturb the wildlife.

reading.title: The Footprints in the Snow
reading.text:
Ravi had never seen snow before his family moved to the mountains. On the first snowy morning, he pressed his nose against the window and gasped. The garden had vanished under a thick white blanket, smooth and silent.
Then he noticed the footprints. They began beside the shed, crossed the garden in a wobbly line and disappeared under the hedge. Each print was small and round, with four tiny toe marks.
“A monster!” whispered his little sister, Priya.
“Monsters have bigger feet,” said Ravi, who was trying to sound brave. He pulled on his boots and followed the trail. It led under the hedge, along the lane and up to the door of the old barn.
Inside, curled up on a pile of straw, was a grey fox with three cubs pressed against her side. She lifted her head and watched them calmly.
Ravi and Priya backed away without a sound. That evening, they left a bowl of water by the barn door, and the next morning it was empty.

c: His family had just moved to the mountains.

reading.title: The Story of Paper
reading.text:
Today, paper is everywhere: in books, boxes, tickets and tissues. But for most of history, people wrote on other materials, such as clay tablets, animal skins and the papyrus plant.
The first true paper was made in China around 2,000 years ago. Papermakers soaked tree bark, old rope and rags in water, beat them into a mushy pulp and spread the pulp thinly on a screen. When it dried, it became a smooth, light sheet that was cheaper than silk and easier to carry than bamboo.
For hundreds of years, the Chinese kept their method a secret. Slowly, the skill travelled west along trade routes. By the eighth century, papermakers were working in Baghdad, and the city became famous for its libraries.
Modern paper is made in huge factories, mainly from wood. Because so many trees are used, recycling paper is important. One tonne of recycled paper can save around seventeen trees.
